Record the assessment in writing, in the standard Alderbridge format, signed and dated by the competent person who completed it.

Communicate the assessment's findings and any control measure to every member of staff involved in the activity, not only file it centrally.

Review the assessment at least annually, or sooner following an incident, a near miss, or any change to the activity, the people involved, or the environment.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where an entirely new, unforeseen activity arises with no existing assessment (for example, a one-off event), a brief, proportionate assessment is completed before the activity begins, even if less formally documented than a standing assessment, rather than the activity proceeding with no risk consideration at all simply because no template already exists for it.

Local and regional variations

The risk assessment methodology and format are standardised across every site; what varies locally is the content of a site's own specific assessments, reflecting its own building, activities and resident group.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This procedure underpins the Health and Safety Policy Statement's wider framework, and the specific risk assessment types referenced throughout other policies — the moving and handling risk assessment, the fire risk assessment, the individual pregnancy risk assessment — all follow this procedure's own core methodology, applied to their specific subject matter.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates proportionate assessment. Introducing a new outdoor sensory garden activity at Harbour View prompts a risk assessment considering uneven ground, weather exposure, and supervision ratios; rather than an exhaustive, generic template, the assessment focuses specifically on the real hazards this particular activity and this particular resident group present, resulting in three practical control measures (non-slip pathway matting, a weather-check-before-starting rule, and a minimum two-staff supervision ratio) rather than a long, generic list of theoretical hazards that do not genuinely apply to this specific activity.

Frequently asked questions

**Who decides if a risk assessment needs a specialist rather than the registered manager?** The registered manager makes this judgement based on the complexity and nature of the risk, escalating to the Health and Safety Lead where genuinely unsure. **What if staff disagree with a control measure a risk assessment specifies?** They raise it with the registered manager or the competent person who completed the assessment; a risk assessment is reviewed and can be corrected, but is not simply ignored informally by an individual member of staff who disagrees with it. **How is a risk assessment different from a care plan?** A risk assessment addresses a hazard to anyone potentially affected by an activity; a care plan addresses an individual person's own specific needs and preferences — the two are related but distinct, and some individual risks (for example, an individual moving and handling risk assessment) sit at the intersection of both.

Training and competency

Registered managers and deputies complete risk assessment training covering the methodology this procedure sets out, and any member of staff completing a specialist assessment (for example, fire risk) holds the relevant additional qualification for that specific area.

Monitoring and compliance

The Health and Safety Lead reviews a sample of risk assessments across sites quarterly for quality and currency, and any site with a significant number of overdue reviews is supported with a targeted catch-up plan.

Record keeping and retention

Risk assessments are retained per the Records Retention Schedule, with the current version readily accessible to staff at the point of the activity it covers, not filed away separately from day-to-day practice.

Approval and review history

This procedure was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 August 2025 and is scheduled for its next full review on 1 August 2026.

sources.title: Risk Assessment Procedure
sources.text:
Risk Assessment Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group identifies, assesses and controls risk across every activity, from a routine task to a significant change in how a site operates. It applies to every site, every activity, and every person who could be affected — staff, people supported, visitors and contractors.

Policy statement

A risk assessment is treated as a genuinely useful working tool that shapes how a task is actually done, not a paperwork exercise completed once and then filed away unread; this procedure is designed around that principle at every stage.

Definitions

**Hazard** anything with the potential to cause harm. **Risk** the likelihood and severity of harm actually occurring from a hazard. **Control measure** an action taken to reduce a risk to an acceptable level. **Competent person** someone with sufficient training, knowledge and experience to complete a risk assessment for a given activity. **Suitable and sufficient** the legal standard a risk assessment must meet — genuinely proportionate to the risk, not exhaustive for its own sake.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** ensures every significant activity at their site has a current risk assessment and that staff are aware of its content. **A competent person** (which may be the registered manager, a trained deputy, or an external specialist for a complex risk) completes the assessment itself. **Every member of staff** follows the control measures a risk assessment specifies and reports any concern that a control is not working in practice.

Identify the hazards present in the activity being assessed, walking through it in practice rather than relying on assumption alone.

Identify who might be harmed and how — staff, people supported, visitors, contractors — considering anyone with a particular vulnerability specifically.

Evaluate the existing controls already in place and whether they are adequate, recording the residual risk honestly rather than understating it.

Identify any further control measure needed to reduce the risk to an acceptable level, recording it with a named owner and a target date.

Health and Safety Executive. **Competent person** someone with sufficient training, knowledge and
experience to carry out a specific health and safety task, which is not the same as simply being willing to
do it.

Organisation and roles

**The Chief Executive** holds overall, ultimate responsibility for health and safety across Alderbridge Care
Group, and personally receives the quarterly health and safety report. **The Health and Safety Lead**, a
dedicated role reporting to the Chief Executive, coordinates policy, training and incident trend analysis
across all sites. **Each registered manager** is responsible for health and safety at their own site day to
day, including ensuring risk assessments are current and staff are trained. **A nominated site health and
safety representative** at each site supports the registered manager, conducts routine walk-round checks,
and is a point of contact for any staff concern. **Every employee** has a personal legal duty to take
reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others affected by what they do, and to
cooperate with Alderbridge in meeting its own duties.

1. Risk assessments are completed for every significant activity before it begins, reviewed annually or
sooner following an incident or a change, per the Risk Assessment Procedure.

2. Every new starter completes a health and safety induction covering fire exits, first aid provision, the
accident and incident reporting process, and any activity-specific risk (for example, lone working or manual
handling) relevant to their role.

3. Every accident, incident and near miss is reported using the Accident and Incident Report Form,
regardless of whether it appears minor, so that patterns can be identified before a more serious incident
occurs.

4. A RIDDOR-reportable incident is escalated to the Health and Safety Lead immediately and reported to
the Health and Safety Executive within the statutory timescale.

5. Equipment used in care delivery (hoists, slings, wheelchairs) is inspected on the schedule set out in the
Equipment Inspection Schedule, and taken out of use immediately if a fault is found, never used pending a
later scheduled check.

Appendix: the five steps at a glance

For quick reference: identify hazards; identify who might be harmed; evaluate existing controls and residual risk; identify further action needed; record, communicate and review.

Assessing risk for a person with fluctuating needs

Where a person's needs fluctuate significantly (for example, a condition with good and bad days), the risk assessment records the range of presentation rather than a single snapshot, and staff are trained to recognise which end of that range they are seeing on a given day so the correct control measure is applied at the right time rather than a single fixed approach being used regardless of how the person actually presents that day.

Risk assessment for one-off events and visits

A one-off event (a fundraising open day, an external visit) receives its own proportionate risk assessment covering the event's specific hazards, completed with enough lead time to put any necessary control in place, rather than being run under a standing, unrelated risk assessment that does not actually address what is different about the event.

When a risk assessment reveals a risk that cannot be adequately controlled

Where an assessment finds a risk that cannot be reduced to an acceptable level with any available control, the activity does not proceed in that form; the registered manager and, where relevant, the Health and Safety Lead consider whether the activity can be modified to remove the unacceptable element, or whether it should not proceed at all, rather than proceeding regardless because stopping the activity feels operationally inconvenient.
